questions.scenario: Masco buys a ৳5 crore knitting line. On the P&L that month, the purchase creates:
options: A ৳5 crore expense
Almost NO expense — cash became an ASSET (Fixed Asset); expense arrives gradually as depreciation over useful life
Revenue of ৳5 crore
A liability of ৳5 crore forever
questions.explanation: Matching principle: the machine serves ten years, so its cost spreads across those years as depreciation. The MD saw cash leave; the P&L correctly shows an asset — Module 11 will reconcile the two views.
wrongExplanations: Expensing day-one would destroy March AND every future month's honesty.
Buying a machine earns nothing by itself.
If paid in cash there's no liability at all — just asset swap.

questions.scenario: The four inputs of any depreciation calculation are:
options: Color, weight, brand, warranty
Cost (incl. installation), useful life, residual value, method
Buyer name, LC number, B/L date, port
Salary, department, attendance, bonus
questions.explanation: Everything needed: what it cost to be READY, how long it serves, what remains at end, and how slices are shaped (straight-line vs declining).
wrongExplanations: Those describe the machine physically, not economically.
That's export documentation (Module 7).
That's payroll data (Module 8).

questions.scenario: Machine cost ৳2,40,00,000, residual ৳20L, straight-line over 11 years. MONTHLY depreciation ≈:
questions.explanation: (2,40,00,000 − 20,00,000) ÷ 11 = ৳20L/year → ÷12 ≈ ৳1,66,667/month. Residual is EXCLUDED from depreciable base; life divides YEARS first.
wrongExplanations: That's the ANNUAL figure — you divided by 11 but not by 12.
You forgot to subtract residual value before dividing.
Off by a factor-of-ten slip — recheck the division.

questions.scenario: Where does knitting machine depreciation flow before touching garment cost?
options: Straight into COGS per tee manually
Into the factory overhead pool, then applied to products via drivers like machine hours
Into export revenue as a deduction
It never reaches product cost
questions.explanation: Same pipes as Module 5: pooled OH applied by usage drivers. Every garment pays machine rent proportional to the machine time it actually consumed.
wrongExplanations: Manual per-tee allocation would be arbitrary and untraceable.
Depreciation is a cost input, not a revenue adjustment.
Ignoring it underprices every garment and overstates profit — the classic factory trap.

questions.scenario: 'Accumulated Depreciation' on the balance sheet represents:
options: Cash saved for replacement machines
The running total of cost already expensed — deducted from asset COST to show BOOK VALUE
The machine's current market price
A liability owed to the machine vendor
questions.explanation: Cost minus accumulated depreciation = book value (e.g., 5Cr − 54L after year one = 4.46Cr). It's memory of allocation, NOT a piggy bank.
wrongExplanations: Depreciation generates no cash — replacement funding comes from retained profits/financing decisions.
Books track allocated COST served, not resale mood.
Vendor was paid long ago; this account faces inward to the asset.

questions.scenario: Which payment gets CAPITALIZED into an asset's cost?
options: Monthly electricity for the hall where it runs
Shipping + installation + trial-run costs needed to make it operational
The operator's salary
Annual maintenance contract
questions.explanation: All costs necessary to bring the asset to working condition join its cost base. Running costs (power, salaries, routine maintenance) remain period expenses.
wrongExplanations: Running costs help production generally — they're OH expenses.
Labor is already routed via Module 8's fork.
Recurring service keeps it RUNNING, didn't make it READY — expense.

questions.scenario: A ৳9L motor rebuild extends the dyeing machine's life by 4 years. Treatment:
options: Expense immediately as repairs
Capitalize — major overhaul extending useful life adds to asset value / replaces component, then depreciates over remaining life
Charge to H&M as claim
Ignore — machines fix themselves
questions.explanation: The test: does spending ADD future benefit (extends life/capacity)? Then capitalize. Routine oil-and-belt servicing merely MAINTAINS — that stays expense. Two repair-looking costs, two different treatments.
wrongExplanations: That would distort this year AND understate assets for four extra years.
Claims belong to buyer disputes (Module 13).
Accounting for wishful thinking is still on the roadmap.

questions.scenario: Old machine fully depreciated to residual ৳50L sells for ৳65L. The sale creates:
options: Revenue of ৳65L
No entry — it was free now
Gain on disposal ৳15L vs book value, with asset and accumulated depreciation removed from books
A new fixed asset of ৳65L
questions.explanation: Book value 50L vs proceeds 65L = 15L disposal gain (other income). Selling a used machine isn't 'revenue' — revenue is from ordinary business; disposals are their own line.
wrongExplanations: Revenue lines are reserved for the trade we're in — selling garments, not machines.
Disposal always needs entries: remove cost, remove accumulated depreciation, record cash, compute gain/loss.
The machine LEFT the company — nothing new was acquired.

questions.scenario: Physical verification finds a registered machine missing since 2023, still being depreciated. Consequence:
options: Keep depreciating — paperwork is sacred
Investigate & derecognize per policy — depreciating ghost assets silently inflates every garment's cost and misstates assets
Buy a duplicate to match records
Ask the supplier to send another invoice
questions.explanation: This is why annual verification exists: registers must mirror reality. Ghost assets overstate both the balance sheet and OH rates feeding pricing — double dishonesty.
wrongExplanations: Faithfully depreciating fiction is worse than admitting loss earlier.
Purchasing to appease paperwork is accounting horror-story material.
Supplier invoices document purchases, not disappearances.

questions.scenario: Rafiq builds the depreciation engine. Which design detail makes audits smooth and costing fair?
options: One giant annual depreciation journal posted each December
Asset register subledger (asset-wise data incl. location/custodian) + monthly scheduled runs with proration for mid-month additions/disposals + automatic OH routing per asset class
Random monthly amounts averaging out
Depreciation only when someone remembers
questions.explanation: Register = subledger truth (Module 3 pattern); schedules = matching across time; class-based routing feeds correct pools (Module 5/8 fork logic). Auditors walk ANY month back to any asset in seconds.
wrongExplanations: December mega-journals wreck every interim month's accuracy.
Randomness is the one thing worse than laziness here.
Memory-based accounting fails exactly when auditors ask 'show me March'.
